https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyl.text: Image source, AFP Image caption, Nirmal Purja became known internationally following a 2021 Netflix documentary By Tinshui Yeung Published 1 August 2026 Renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja is among 10 people killed in an avalanche on Broad Peak in Pakistan, his company has said. Elite Expeditions said it confirmed with "profound sadness and immense heartbreak" that Purja, 43, had died in Thursday's avalanche. His brother Kamal later wrote: "We will miss you every single day". Purja, who was born in Nepal and later served in the British army, was known for scaling the world's 14 highest peaks in just over six months in 2019. Pakistani officials earlier said the bodies of three climbers from his expedition - American Mallory Geis, Nadhira Ahmed Abdullah Al Harthy from Oman and Pur Bahadur Gurung from Nepal - had been recovered. Figure caption, Renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja confirmed dead in Pakistan avalanche Purja's death was also confirmed by Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, who said that "the tragic death of six Nepalese and four other foreign climbers, including world record holder Nirmal Purja, in the Karakoram mountain range of Pakistan, has shocked us". "The history of their courage, dedication, and contributions will always remain inspiring," the prime minister added. In a statement, Purja's older brother Kamal wrote: "It is with the heaviest heart that I share the devastating news that my beloved younger brother, Nirmal 'Nimsdai' Purja, and the other climbers are no longer with us. "Although our hearts are broken, we are incredibly proud of you. Your legacy will live forever," he added. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a post on X: "Incredibly sad to learn of the passing of Nirmal (Nims) Purja and those he was climbing with. "He was an inspirational man who served in our Armed Forces for many years - and whose incredible mountaineering adventures are known the world over." Naila Kiani, a spokesperson for the Alpine Club of Pakistan which is involved in the rescue efforts, told BBC's Newshour programme that Purja had led many expeditions that she was on. Praising his leadership skills, she described him as a "very experienced climber and fearless". Kiani said the Alpine Club would only announce his death once the body has been recovered - but she added that "we are fearing them all dead". She also said rescuers had seen some bodies - but were yet to reach them. Teams in Pakistan have been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit after an avalanche on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range. The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja. Also known as Nims, he rose to prominence in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains with peaks above 8,000m in 189 days - smashing the previous record by more than seven years. He became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released two years later. At the time, he said: "It has been a gruelling but humbling six months, and I hope to have proven that anything is possible with some determination, self-belief and positivity." Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering. Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military. In his last post on X, published on Monday, he said he had not intended to climb Broad Peak. "Initially, the plan was to climb just G2," Purja wrote, referring to Gasherbrum II, another peak in the Karakoram mountain range. But right before he set off for Pakistan, he realised that if he also managed to climb Broad Peak while he was there, he would have only one more mountain to conquer before becoming the "first person in history to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice. Without oxygen." An eight-thousander is a mountain that rises more than 8,000m above sea level. "This wasn't planned," Purja wrote. "But opportunities don't scream: they whisper to those already working in silence." "Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted," he wrote. Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit. Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives. One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella says the operations against ‘illegal immigrants’ will involve police and the migration authority. Photograph: Pablo R Seco/EPA View image in fullscreen Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella says the operations against ‘illegal immigrants’ will involve police and the migration authority. Photograph: Pablo R Seco/EPA Colombia Colombia’s new president Abelardo de la Espriella announces immigration crackdown Far-right leader echoes ally Donald Trump and says operations to ‘track down illegal immigrants’ should begin this week, amid earthquake aftermath Tiago Rogero South America correspondent Mon 24 Aug 2026 20.34 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced a crackdown on immigrants, ordering authorities to detain and deport people who are in the country irregularly or have committed crimes. In office for just over two weeks, the millionaire former lawyer made the announcement on Sunday as the country continued to grapple with the aftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake on 10 August that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes. De la Espriella said the first joint operations involving the police and the migration authority should begin “this very week”. “Let the coordinated operations begin to track down illegal immigrants: first, those committing crimes; second, those who have not regularised their status and who will have to be deported immediately,” de la Espriella said during a cabinet meeting held on Sunday in Barranquilla, the Caribbean city that has in effect been turned into an alternative capital. US promises $1bn in security aid to Colombia as new rightwing president pledges drugs crackdown Read more He echoed the “Americans first” rhetoric of his ally, US president Donald Trump , saying that from now on it would be “Colombians first, Colombians second and Colombians third”. The Colombian president has joined other Trump-aligned leaders in the region who have also tightened migration rules, including Argentina’s Javier Milei and Chile’s José Antonio Kast. De la Espriella’s order is facing criticism from the opposition and human rights activists, who say it will end a migration policy that endured for more than a decade under both rightwing and leftwing governments and benefited above all migrants fleeing the humanitarian crisis in neighbouring Venezuela. Although he used the anti-immigration rhetoric characteristic of other far-right candidates during his campaign, his platform focused chiefly on his promise to pursue an iron-fist policy against criminal groups. In the same announcement, he also declared that all gangs involved in drug trafficking, illegal mining, extortion and smuggling were “terrorists and we will treat them as such. Whatever happens, we will defeat them, by reason or by force.” The president did not directly mention Venezuelans when discussing immigration, but they account for roughly 90% of all migrants in the country. Of the 2.8 million Venezuelans living in Colombia, about 848,000 are in an irregular situation, including 193,000 children and adolescents. Activist forced out of US after criticising Trump-aligned Colombian politician Read more The leftwing senator María José Pizarro Rodríguez reposted the president’s announcement and asked whether he was “proposing a Colombian ICE against fellow Latin Americans”, in reference to the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). She added that the “order to deport irregular migrants is pure xenophobia and aporophobia”. “Instead of persecuting people fleeing poverty and violence, regularise their status. There are thousands of migrants who work hard and contribute to the economies of the countries that receive them,” she wrote. The Colombian newspaper El Tiempo reported that sources within the migration department believe the agency does not have enough staff to carry out the operations De la Espriella has promised. Analysts have also noted that under Colombian law there is no such category as an “illegal” immigrant, as De la Espriella said, but rather migrants in an “irregular” situation, since being in the country without the proper documentation is not a crime. https://www.politico.eu/article/far-righ.text: BRUSSELS — A possible string of far-right election victories next year could derail efforts to boost the European Union’s standing in international climate talks. An EU plan to wield more influence over the annual United Nations climate conferences will be put to the test from Monday, when this year’s COP31 conference begins in the Turkish city of Antalya. The bloc hopes to build up negotiating clout in time for the pivotal summit in 2028, when countries will face off over measures to step up global pollution-slashing efforts. Advertisement Advertisement But there’s a risk that the EU’s unity on international climate issues will crumble before next year’s COP32 rolls around. Over the next 12 months, four of the bloc’s five largest countries — France, Spain, Italy and Poland — will hold closely contested elections where far-right and populist parties are expected to score high. Politicians from those camps made their disdain for the U.N. climate process plain in a European Parliament debate last month. “This COP will be a failure, like the previous ones,” said Marie-Luce Brasier-Clain, a lawmaker for the far-right party National Rally, whose candidate Marine Le Pen is the front-runner in France’s presidential election. A sign is seen near the entrance of the Antalya Expo venue, where COP31 will take place, on Sept. 30, 2026. | Goksel Yapar/AFP via Getty Images “It's because you're pursuing an ideological agenda that cannot be implemented, on the basis of the Paris accords, without there being mass deindustrialization and social upheaval,” she told EU officials present at the debate. “Summit after summit, we see leaders taking private jets in order to explain that this big environmental problem is actually caused by tractors, that's what they tell the farmers,” said Mireia Borrás Pabón, a lawmaker from Spain’s far-right Vox, which hopes to enter a coalition with conservatives after the country’s November election. “Their priority, it seems, would be to eliminate fossil fuels… What does that mean? It means everything is more expensive,” she claimed. "Who do you think the COP really serves? Because it’s clear it’s not Europeans." Advertisement Advertisement Far-right and right-wing MEPs from Poland, Germany and Austria echoed their views. At home, those parties are campaigning to slash national and EU measures to reduce emissions and scale back development aid, including for climate action abroad — changes that would undermine the bloc’s sway at COPs just as it seeks to solidify its leadership position. Centrist politicians see the risk, but they haven’t given up hope. “We have been seeing the United States turning the back on the fight for climate change and also climate science, and I could be worried that we also will see other countries also within the European Union take the same path,” Danish Climate Minister Samira Nawa told POLITICO. But the victory of many pro-climate Democrats in the U.S. midterms might signal a shift, she added. “Hopefully we can see the same within Europe.” Strategic shift EU governments vowed to step up their diplomatic efforts after they were left isolated at last year’s COP30 in Brazil. Ministers met several times earlier this year to discuss how the EU could improve its conference preparations, as well as its messaging. “There's been a lot of work during the past year, both during the Cyprus presidency [of the Council of the EU] and now during the Irish presidency to ensure that we become even better prepared,” said Mattias Frumerie, Sweden’s climate ambassador. The outcome was a tighter negotiating stance, a decision to cluster all country pavilions in the conference event space into a single “EU village” to project greater influence and a first-ever joint communications strategy for COP31 to speak with one voice. Advertisement Advertisement “COP31 will be a contest of narratives as much as a negotiation,” reads the strategy, seen by POLITICO. The EU should position itself as “constructive, not confrontational… confident, not triumphalist… listening, not lecturing… forward-looking, not defensive… multilateral, not transactional… relatable and accessible.” The EU and its governments have also sought to build alliances and increase their outreach ahead of COP31, diplomats say. The idea is to treat the annual negotiations as a long game, looking ahead at what’s known as the second Global Stocktake (GST2) in 2028 — an exercise to assess progress toward the Paris Agreement's goals and course-correct where necessary. The first such stocktake in 2023 resulted in a landmark agreement to transition away from fossil fuels. The Danish Alternative party climate change-themed election posters hang outside Christiansborg Palace on Oct. 22, 2022. | James Brooks/AFP via Getty Images “The intent… is to start looking at a multi-annual approach to how COP is done by the EU, start looking towards GST2 and try to see the longer-term program that we have,” a senior European climate negotiator said. Political and economic trends across the EU, however, risk undermining those efforts. “We’re seeing it partly already … just from the conversations we’ve had in the past couple of months, which have been quite public as well, that some member states sense that the policies that we put in place to drive the transition are becoming too costly for their companies,” Frumerie said. Advertisement Advertisement Price pressures and the rise of the far right are pushing many governments toward a more cautious stance on climate policy. Shrinking fiscal space is also pushing many European countries to cut back on overseas aid, putting their contributions to the global climate finance goal agreed at COP29 at risk. Funding from developed countries for developing nations is a core principle of fairness in the U.N. talks, and frustrations over looming shortfalls tend to obstruct agreement on the kind of ambitious climate action demanded by the EU. A string of far-right victories over the coming year could supercharge those shifts. Ballot bonanza The first major election takes place just after COP31 wraps, on Nov. 29 in Spain. The conservative People’s Party, leading the polls, is in talks to enter a coalition with the far-right Vox to replace a Socialist government that has overseen a surge in renewable energy deployment and pushed for ambitious climate action at the EU level. Vox has called for a widespread rollback of the European Green Deal and in a 2025 policy program demanded Spain’s withdrawal from the Paris Agreement while supporting a “disengagement” from COP decisions. While the People’s Party hasn’t adopted such strong positions, it has teamed up with the far right to block climate action in the past, for example in a failed bid to veto the EU’s new 2040 emissions-cutting goal . Next up is France, which will hold a presidential election in April and May next year. Advertisement Advertisement Le Pen, who leads the polls by a large margin, recently pledged to “achieve carbon neutrality by 2050 and comply with the Paris Agreement” in a speech aimed at reassuring financial markets about her candidacy . She has also sought to distance herself from her far-right party’s history of climate denialism. But her party wants to axe €2.1 billion in development aid, including climate finance, and repeal a law that bans drilling for new oil and gas reserves on French soil — a move at odds with international commitments to cut back on fossil fuels. It also wants to impose a moratorium on new solar and wind farms, betting mostly on nuclear energy. “We need to build strategic [oil and gas] reserves and secure supplies while we wait for the electrification of energy use,” National Rally lawmaker Alexandre Loubet told POLITICO. “There is natural gas in my constituency, but the government refuses to exploit it.” A demonstrator holds a large sign during a procession in Paris on Oct. 31, 2026. | Laurent Caron/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images After the summer, Poland will head to the polls, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s center-right coalition trying to fight off the nationalist Law and Justice Party. Under Tusk, Poland has invested in accelerating its switch away from coal and stepped up its involvement in COPs — in Antalya, as last year, its minister has been asked by the conference hosts to co-lead global talks on ensuring a fair energy transition. Meanwhile, the PiS fiercely campaigns against core EU climate policies and wants to retain the country’s coal generation. It has cast the bloc as misguided and isolated on the global stage. “We are negotiating with the whole world [at COP31], so we need to answer a couple of questions. Why are we alone as the European Union? Why won't the world contribute to the implementation of those ambitions?” said PiS lawmaker Anna Zalewska at the European Parliament debate. Advertisement Finally, Italy will vote before the end of the year. Right-wing Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who is aiming for a second term, has used her COP appearances to condemn “environmental radicalism” and has sought to weaken core EU climate policies, but has remained broadly supportive of diplomatic efforts. “Depending on the outcome of the elections, it doesn't make the situation for and within the EU easier,” Ottmar Edenhofer, a German economist who advises the bloc on climate policy, told reporters in a pre-COP press conference. Still, Denmark’s Nawa expressed hope that any party winning elections in Europe would try to “make a secure life for people all around the world but also within the European Union.” “No matter what government, no matter what politicians are in power,” she said, “we have to solve these crises.” Nicolas Camut contributed reporting from Paris.
